transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you here today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a bit complicated to explain, but it's really starting to mess with my job. I'm a construction manager, you see, and I've been doing this for over twenty years. Started from the bottom, worked my way up. I've been on hundreds of sites, maybe thousands, seen it all. But lately, I’m here because every time I have to get near a scaffold, roof edge, or upper platform now, my head just... it just tells me I’m about to go over. And the crazy thing is, I know it's safe. I'm the one who checks the safety protocols! I can see the rails are in place, I know the setup is supposed to be safe, I know the guys who built it, I know the materials. But my brain just screams at me that I'm going to fall, that the edge is just pulling me over. It's not like a normal fear of heights, it's this overwhelming certainty that I'm going to plunge to the ground, even when I'm standing behind a solid barrier. It's getting so bad I can't even do my walk-throughs properly anymore, and if I can't get up there to inspect the work, I can't do my job, and I've got a crew relying on me, deadlines to meet, and this whole thing is just... it's exhausting, honestly.

Have you ever experienced sudden episodes where your heart races, you feel short of breath, or feel like something terrible is going to happen when you're near these heights or even thinking about them?

Oh, absolutely, it's... it's like a switch just flips in my body. I mean, just the other day we were at the new commercial build downtown—it's a great project, a five-story mixed-use thing, but the elevators aren't in yet, obviously. So we have these temporary stairs set up. Good, sturdy metal stairs, bolted in exactly to code. I checked the specs myself. But the second, and I mean the absolute *second* I step onto those temporary stairs, or even just walk toward an open upper floor where the exterior walls aren't up yet... it hits me all at once. 

My chest tightens up so bad it feels like there's a steel band wrapped right around my ribs. And my hands—I wear these heavy-duty grip gloves, right?—my hands get so wet inside them, just completely drenched in sweat, which is dangerous on its own if you actually needed to grab a rail. But the craziest part is my legs. I'll just be standing there, looking up at the next landing, and I feel like my legs might completely lock up on me before I can even make myself take another step. They just turn to lead. 

And you asked about feeling like something terrible is going to happen—that's exactly it. My brain is just flashing these images of me going over the side, and I'm standing there with my chest squeezing, trying to pull air in, and I literally can't force my boots to move forward. And, you know, my crew is up there waiting for me to sign off on the framing, and I'm stuck at the bottom of the stairs, gripping the rail with wet hands, feeling like I'm fighting for my life against absolutely nothing. It's just so frustrating because I know how ridiculous it looks, a guy my size, twenty years on the job, frozen on a perfectly good staircase...
Has this kind of intense physical and mental reaction ever happened to you in situations that don't involve being up high or near an edge?

No, no, never. That's the thing that's so baffling about all of this. It's strictly—I mean, 100 percent—tied to the heights and the edges. If I'm on the ground floor, or even just in a regular building that's completely closed in, like an office building where the windows don't open, I'm right as rain. I can handle stress, doc. I mean, my job is basically just managing one crisis after another. Deliveries are late, subcontractors don't show up, the weather turns and ruins a concrete pour... I deal with high-pressure situations all day long, and my heart rate doesn't even spike. I don't get sweaty, I don't freeze up. I just get on the radio and fix it. 

Even outside of work, I'm a pretty relaxed guy. I don't get worked up in traffic, I don't get nervous in crowds or tight spaces or anything like that. I fly on planes without a second thought. My wife and I, we went to Florida last year, flew down, smooth as silk, didn't bother me at all. But put me on a half-finished third floor of a condo project with temporary guardrails, and suddenly I'm a mess. It's like my body only has this one specific trigger. If my boots are on solid, enclosed ground, I'm the guy everyone else comes to when they're panicking. But the second I have to step near a drop-off... it's just that one very specific thing that sets off all these alarms in my head.
Do you start feeling anxious or panicky even when you're just thinking about going up high or approaching an edge, before you actually get there?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I've been paying a lot of attention to exactly when the feeling starts. It's not just when I'm standing right on the edge, looking down. It actually starts way before that. Like, I'll be sitting in my truck in the morning, drinking my coffee, going over the punch list for the day, and I'll see that I need to go up to the fourth floor to check the HVAC installation. And just reading the words 'fourth floor' on my clipboard... my stomach does this little flip. 

And then, as I'm walking across the site, heading toward the building, I can feel my heart rate start to pick up. It's like a slow build, you know? By the time I'm putting on my hard hat and walking toward the stairwell, I'm already starting to feel that tightness in my chest. I'm already thinking about the drop, about how high up it is, about what could go wrong. It's like my brain is trying to warn me away from the danger before I'm even close to it. 

I remember last Tuesday, I had to inspect a roof deck that was being poured. I knew about it all weekend. And I swear to you, doc, Sunday night, I was sitting on my couch watching the game, and the thought of that roof deck popped into my head, and my palms actually started sweating right there in my living room. Just the anticipation of it, just knowing I was going to have to face it in a couple of days, was enough to set me off. So yeah, it definitely starts before I even get there. It's like the fear is waiting for me, and the closer I get, the louder it gets. It's exhausting, just constantly dreading the next time I have to go up.
Do you find yourself actively avoiding going up high or doing things that might involve being near an edge, even if it affects your work or daily routine?

Well, yeah, I mean... I'm doing everything I possibly can to get out of it, and it's starting to become a real problem. I've been a construction manager for a long time, and a big part of the job is supposed to be having eyes on every single aspect of the build, right? But lately, I've been... well, I've been handing off a lot of the height inspections to my foremen. I'll just tell them, "Hey, I need you to go check the framing on the fifth floor, I've got a mountain of paperwork down here in the trailer," which, you know, there's always paperwork, so it sounds like a legitimate excuse. But they're starting to notice. You can't just keep delegating the high-up stuff without the guys on the crew putting two and two together. 

And it's not just inspections. I've been moving all my meetings to the ground level. Used to be, if we had an issue on the third floor, I'd bring the architect and the structural guy right up there, we'd stand on the deck, point at the problem, and figure it out. Now? Now I'm telling them to meet me in the office trailer, and we're looking at blueprints spread out on a folding table instead of actually looking at the physical structure. It's not as efficient, and honestly, it's not how I like to run my sites. 

But sometimes, I mean, sometimes there's just no way around it. The owner of the development company comes out, or the city inspector insists I walk the upper floors with him. When I absolutely have to go up, it's... it's an ordeal. I'll make sure I have one of my biggest guys, like my lead carpenter, walk right beside me, on the side closest to the edge, like a human shield almost. And I just rush through it. I don't look around, I don't take my time to really inspect the work like I should. I just keep my eyes glued to the decking, say "Looks good, looks good," and get back to the stairs as fast as humanly possible. And the whole time, my heart is pounding out of my chest, I'm sweating through my shirt, and I'm just absolutely terrified until my boots hit the ground floor again. It's exhausting, doc. It's really starting to mess with how I do my job.
Do you ever worry that you might have another panic attack in a height-related situation, or feel anxious about the possibility of it happening again?

Well, I... I don't know if I'd call it a worry about the panic attack itself, exactly. I mean, I'm not sitting around thinking, "Oh boy, I hope my heart doesn't start pounding again." It's more just... I'm worried about the heights, period. The whole experience of being up there is what I dread. The sweating, the shaking, the feeling like I'm going to fall—that's all just part of the package, you know? 

Like, when I'm looking at the schedule and I see I have to do a roof inspection next week, my brain doesn't go, "Watch out, you might have a panic attack." It goes, "You have to go up high, and it's going to be terrible." It's the situation itself that I'm terrified of. The physical stuff that happens to me when I'm up there—it's awful, don't get me wrong, it's absolutely miserable—but it's so tied to the height that I don't really separate the two in my head. I'm just dreading being near the edge. If I could somehow go up there and not feel that way, that'd be great, but since I know I will, I just worry about having to go up in the first place. Does that make sense? It's the heights that are the enemy, not necessarily my body's reaction to them, even though the reaction is what makes it so impossible to deal with.
